column1: hybrid-encryption|B|B11|tls|Why do many secure protocols use public-key mechanisms plus symmetric traffic keys?|Asymmetric methods establish/authenticate key material; symmetric encryption protects bulk data|Every payload byte must be encrypted with RSA directly|Symmetric encryption authenticates every certificate chain|Public-key signatures compress all transmitted files|Hybrid design separates key establishment, authentication, and efficient bulk protection. Exact mechanisms vary by protocol.|An algorithm's role matters as much as its name.

mac-replay|B|B11|password|A valid HMAC-protected request is replayed unchanged. What may still be missing?|Freshness or anti-replay state|Integrity of the original authenticated bytes|Knowledge of the HMAC key by the legitimate sender|A deterministic verification procedure|A valid tag does not establish that a message is new. Nonces, sequence numbers, timestamps, and receiver state can address replay.|Authentication and freshness are different properties.

forward-secrecy|B|B12|tls|Why can ephemeral key agreement improve forward secrecy?|Later compromise of a long-term key need not reveal past traffic keys|It prevents every future private-key theft|It removes all need for peer authentication|It guarantees application data is never logged|Past-session confidentiality depends on ephemeral-secret handling and protocol design. Long-term identity protection is another concern.|Forward secrecy does not promise endpoint secrecy.

certificate-name|B|B12|tlscheat|A certificate is valid for one hostname but served from several IPs. What does hostname validation bind?|The intended service name, not one permanent network address|Every address in the provider's allocation|Every application hosted on the same IP|Every user account on the server|Services can change or share addresses. Certificate name validation concerns the intended name under the relevant rules.|Names and routing addresses are related but distinct.

signature-confidentiality|B|B11|tls|A plaintext document has a valid digital signature. Which property is not supplied by signing alone?|Confidentiality of its contents|Detection of modifications to signed content|Verification using the signer's public key|A link to the signing key's identity evidence|Signatures authenticate protected content subject to trusted-key handling. They do not conceal the signed document.|A signed artifact can remain publicly readable.

checksum-adversary|B|B11|hash|Why is an ordinary unkeyed checksum weak against deliberate message replacement?|An attacker can replace both message and checksum|Every checksum requires a private signing key|Checksums automatically establish peer identity|A matching checksum proves authorized origin|Checksums can detect accidental corruption. Adversarial integrity requires authenticated reference values or suitable cryptographic mechanisms.|Accidental-error detection is not adversarial authentication.

network-five-tuple|B|B1|tcp|What distinguishes two simultaneous TCP connections between the same client and server addresses?|Their source/destination ports as part of the flow tuple|Only the application's window title|Only the Ethernet broadcast address|Only whether the data contains HTML|Connections are identified by protocol and endpoint address/port information. Source ports can distinguish concurrent flows.|A host pair is not a complete connection identity.

fragment-observation|B|B5|tcp|A packet capture records only a non-initial IP fragment. What transport information may be absent?|The original transport header and port fields|The IP version field necessarily|Every source and destination address|The existence of any fragment offset|Transport headers normally begin in the initial fragment. Reassembly and capture completeness affect interpretation.|A packet fragment may not be a whole transport message.
